strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem in cognitive NLP: distinguishing brain-conditioned language generation from performance supported by repeated stimuli or familiar subjects. This is directly relevant to interpreting brain-to-text results.

The study examines five splitting strategies across two public datasets, covering both fMRI and EEG and evaluating UniCoRN and EEG2Text. The substantial performance differences provide useful evidence that splitting protocols materially affect reported results.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is appropriate for the stated generalization goal. The conceptual graph formulation, treatment of overlapping fMRI windows, and acknowledgment that enforcing separation discards data provide a useful starting point for benchmark design.
weaknesses: The supplied algorithms do not enforce the central guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, restores edges after checking the subject partition but does not exclude stimuli assigned to validation or test; it can therefore reintroduce text overlap. Algorithm 2, line 33, has the analogous problem for subjects. These may be pseudocode errors, but they must be corrected and reconciled with Table 1's claimed zero leakage using a verifiable implementation.

The experiments do not establish the claimed mechanisms of encoder degradation and decoder memorization. Decreasing reconstruction validation loss does not demonstrate that an encoder is degrading, and improving test scores with additional training is not itself evidence of contamination. Table 2 also changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together. A randomly initialized encoder is not a control that removes signal information. Matched training settings and language-only, shuffled-signal, or noise-input controls are needed to substantiate the claim that accurate generation occurs without meaningful use of brain signals.

The interpretation conflates contamination with changes in the generalization problem. Subject overlap is inappropriate for evaluating unseen-subject generalization, but can be legitimate for personalized decoding. Moreover, the proposed protocol changes subject and stimulus distributions while discarding training data. Without reporting retained data and controlling training-set size, performance differences cannot be attributed specifically to contamination. The criticism of previous protocols should be tied to the generalization claims those protocols support.

The leakage metrics are not sufficiently well defined to reproduce. Equation (7) intersects individual signal samples, whereas its stated purpose concerns shared subject identities: distinct EEG recordings from the same person need not intersect. Its denominator is also zero for entirely held-out subjects, without a specified convention. The counting units and overlap definitions need clarification and reconciliation with Table 1.

Table 3 contains a concrete numerical inconsistency: UniCoRN with 80 epochs under method (c) has ROUGE-1 F = 84.64, precision = 63.16, and recall = 71.50. Under standard consistent aggregation, F cannot exceed their arithmetic mean of 67.33. This result requires correction and an audit of the scoring and reporting pipeline.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are insufficient for the benchmark contribution. Although Appendix A supplies training settings, the manuscript provides no benchmark access link or exact split manifests, post-filtering partition counts, discarded-data fractions, or clear checkpoint-selection and test-time decoding procedures. It should explicitly state whether evaluation supplies any gold prefixes or tokens. The four seeds in Table 1 concern overlap statistics; Tables 2–4 do not report variability in decoding performance. These substantive soundness and reproducibility gaps prevent a Findings recommendation, but focused corrections and controlled reruns could support resubmission next cycle.
